claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 can be produced as rapidly quenched ribbons by melt spinning.
The rapidly quenched alloy exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence under standard thermal treatment.
A millisecond-scale flash-annealing pulse immediately after rapid quenching will improve amorphous retention and thermal stability.
The flash pulse will promote atomic structural relaxation without triggering significant nucleation.
The flash pulse will suppress primary non-eutectic crystallite formation.
A suitable flash-annealing window is approximately 850–900 K, just below the crystallization onset.
The relevant rapid-quench cooling-rate range is approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s.
Immediate post-quench application of the pulse can keep the alloy below the threshold for significant nucleation while permitting atomic relaxation.
Atomic relaxation reduces free volume and internal stresses in the quenched alloy.
Reduced free volume and internal stress diminish the driving force for nucleation of primary crystallites.
The brief pulse homogenizes the local atomic structure.
Pulse-induced structural homogenization, stress relief, and free-volume reduction delay or suppress crystal nucleation during subsequent reheating.
Flash-annealed samples will retain a higher amorphous fraction than untreated rapidly quenched samples.
Flash-annealed samples will have a higher effective crystallization-onset temperature than untreated samples.
Thermal analysis of flash-annealed samples will show reduced primary-crystallization signatures.
Untreated rapidly quenched ribbons undergo extensive primary non-eutectic crystallization during slow cooling and reheating.
Untreated ribbons have a lower apparent crystallization-onset temperature than the predicted flash-annealed state.
Temperature overshoot above the proposed flash window may cause inadvertent nucleation.
